output.headline: UK-EU trade deals set to add £17bn to economy, Burnham says
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham is preparing to unveil billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU, covering everything from youth visas to pet passports, as part of his vision for a much closer relationship with the bloc.

Burnham said on Tuesday that the agreement would boost the UK economy by £17bn – an increase of 0.4%. His advisers believe it will also strengthen his attempts to forge much closer ties with, and even potentially rejoin, the bloc.

With the prime minister scheduled to meet his European counterparts in Brussels on 20 November, officials have all but agreed three deals that would allow farmers to sell freely to the continent and travellers to take their animals abroad more easily.

Although parts of the agreement will not be put in place until 2028, those close to the talks insist the process will not be derailed by disagreements on European industrial policy or UK university fees.

Elements of the deal, which will see the UK pay the EU for access to its emissions trading scheme, face criticism from those who argue Britain is signing up to the same rules it was seeking to avoid when it left the bloc.

The prime minister told the Economist on Tuesday: “A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now that is a number that you cannot ignore.”

And he told ITV: “Public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”

Burnham will meet Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, the president of the European Council, in Brussels later this month when the leaders are expected to announce the deals.

They include an agricultural agreement, which the government believes will be worth over £5bn to the UK economy by 2040; access to the EU’s emissions trading scheme; and a youth visa scheme for tens of thousands of people under 30.

Officials on both sides say the final text for all three deals is close to being agreed, though some key details need to be finalised. These include how many young people should be allowed to travel under the mobility scheme.

Both sides are understood to have agreed that each European member state should get its own quota under the scheme, to spread out the benefits and potential costs.

Under the proposed agricultural deal, UK companies and travellers would no longer have to get a certificate to transport live animals, including pets, into Europe. Those wanting to bring domesticated animals into the bloc would be issued with a pet passport, eradicating the need for complicated paperwork each trip.

UK producers would be allowed to continue selling some products that are banned under EU law, such as certain pesticides, for a “transition period”. Trade in other products, including live molluscs and Scottish salmon, would be freed up.

Under an agreement on emissions, the UK will pay the EU billions of pounds to avoid a cross-border carbon tax, which comes into place next January. Under a separate agreement the UK will join the EU emissions trading scheme to avoid being trapped.

And under the “youth experience scheme”, Britain and the EU would issue visas to people under the age of 30 to live, work and travel in each other’s territories. The UK is negotiating an emergency brake-style mechanism to make sure that if a member state refuses to issue its quota of visas, the UK will restrict the number of their nationals looking to travel to Britain.

Officials on both sides have now started talks over a separate joint statement setting out areas of future cooperation, including on industrial policy and tuition fees. A draft of that agreement seen by the Guardian would seek to conclude an agreement on charging European students lower fees within six months.

The Guardian revealed earlier this week that the UK was willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for any financial loss as a result – but only if the EU agreed to grant Britain access to its protectionist Made in Europe scheme.

The draft statement, which has been prepared by the EU and not yet agreed by the UK, describes the two sides as “trusted partners” – language which the UK believes will allow it to participate in Made in Europe.

But European countries are pushing Britain to sign up to higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a move UK ministers and businesses are resisting. The European draft text says both sides will “cooperate closely and explore further solutions”.

It also says the UK is likely to pay a financial contribution to the EU’s “cohesion” budget to help poorer member states – though this has not been signed off by the UK and is understood to be more likely as part of a future agreement.

The EU has also raised concerns about the UK’s plans for an accelerated programme to deport “foreign national offenders from the UK to the EU”, which it is pushing London to drop.

The agreement being announced later this month forms one half of Burnham’s attempts to reset the British conversation over Europe.

The prime minister is also planning a major announcement setting out his vision for how the UK could interact with the union in the future, including possible re-entry.

Downing Street has said this would take place “around the time of the summit” – though it has not yet been decided whether it will be before, during or after.
output.standfirst: Deals on agriculture, youth visas and emissions are nearly finalised as part of Burnham's plan for closer ties with Brussels, promising a £17bn boost to the economy – though critics say Britain is re-adopting rules it once left.
output.progress: Officials on both sides are finalising deals on agriculture, emissions and youth visas, which EU leaders are expected to announce at a Brussels summit this month.

context.text: France has dropped its opposition to the UK joining the EU's 'Made in Europe' scheme, as long as Britain aligns with the EU's position on tariffs for Chinese electric vehicles.

output.headline: King Charles pledges to 'address past wrongs' of slavery through new partnerships
output.bodyHtml:
King Charles says deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, even as Caribbean leaders and campaigners step up demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.

“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past.

“The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”

Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs.

He pointed to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage, while stopping short of an apology or explicit support for reparations.

“For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.

Though speaking as head of the Commonwealth, and this speech would have been drafted by Charles personally along with his advisers, palace aides have indicated there would be “no surprises” in it for the UK government.

Burnham has said he is open to Britain apologising for slavery, with officials holding talks with national leaders in Antigua about what that could entail.

He has also proposed debt-reset discussions for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

Burnham, though, declined to say whether the UK might offer further financial contributions to the Commonwealth, short of reparations, when pressed by reporters.

The UK prime minister told reporters: “I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations, and I made that quite abundantly clear in the piece that I wrote in advance of coming here.

“But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got, green finance. That’s what we’ve done under all governments, and in my view, we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth.”

Pressed on whether this could mean additional financial contributions that would weigh on the taxpayer, Burnham said: “Well, you’re getting ahead. What we need to have is that meaningful dialogue where we take time to listen, and let’s be clear: the Commonwealth is an important part of our trade too.

“It’s a two-way arrangement. You know, trade is up between the UK and the rest of the Commonwealth in the last year quite significantly, actually. So you need to see it in that way as well. It benefits Britain to be here, listening to people, building that new partnership, and that’s good for growth in Britain.”

Reparations are not formally on the agenda of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), where trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and opportunities for young people were among the stated priorities of the 56-member bloc.

Sustained campaigning by Caribbean governments and a growing international reparations movement have propelled the issue to the centre of political debate surrounding the gathering.

Opening the summit in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, the country’s prime minister, Gaston Browne, said “fairness” required an “honest engagement with our shared history” and called for meaningful and respectful dialogue on reparatory justice and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism.

But Caribbean leaders have stressed that dialogue must extend beyond an apology. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), described an apology as an “essential first step” but said an “apology without repair is incomplete”.

He said any structured dialogue must allow consideration of the entirety of Caricom’s 10-point reparations plan, including public health, education, cultural restitution, psychological rehabilitation, debt cancellation and monetary compensation.

Britain’s royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology. A palace spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the king to announce a change in government policy.

According to the AFP news agency, Burnham discussed slavery with the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral meetings the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.

They discussed how Britain was “offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade”, including the “next steps”, Downing Street said.

Outside the heavily secured summit venue, protesters gathered with placards declaring: “We know what you did and we can see you,” and “You say appalling atrocity, yet you refuse to apologise.”

One protester, Lenworth Johnson, said that if the king’s constitutional position prevented him from apologising, the British government should authorise him to do so. “We feel an apology is necessary,” he said.

Related: UK makes huge aid cuts to Commonwealth nations despite warm words at Chogm

Another, Radcliffe Robins, said the wealth enjoyed by Britain and other western powers was built in part on enslavement. “It is absolutely necessary that his majesty the king and the royal family apologise for the brutality and the injustice that they have imposed on us,” he said. “And with that, we ask for reparations.”

Another protester said the demonstration was intended to ensure those entering the summit knew campaigners were “watching them and listening to what they’re saying and what they’re doing”.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda Reparations Support Commission and one of the organisers, said: “One whose heart is filled with horror and whose soul bears the most profound personal sorrow must surely be moved beyond words – beyond repeated emotional expression without acceptance of responsibility.

“Genuine moral consciousness demands apologies – the acknowledgment of wrong, the acceptance of responsibility and the commitment to pursue reparations. Unfortunately King Charles III does nothing of the sort. He has again failed the people who recognise him as king.”

The demonstrations followed a reparations event on Monday hosted by the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations alongside campaign organisations.

Its chair, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, welcomed debt relief but warned against presenting it as reparations.

“Reparations was never about personal guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions that still stand,” she said. “Aid is not reparations, because aid leaves the power with the giver. Agency was the crime. Agency has to be the remedy.”

The meeting was followed by a candlelight vigil on an Antiguan beach commemorating enslaved Africans brought to the island. The Rev Bonnie Smith, president of the Antigua Christian Council, asked those gathered to remember people torn from their homes, separated from their families and forced across the Atlantic into enslavement.

Related: Memo to King Charles: if the Dutch king can apologise for slavery, why can’t you? | Raoul de Jong

“Their names may be absent from our records, but they are not absent from your love,” she said. “Their voices may have been silenced, but their lives have never ceased to matter.”

Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, meanwhile framed the campaign as part of a wider struggle for peace and justice.

“We are concerned about the unleashing of terror and violence upon innocent people,” he said.

“We believe that reparatory justice that calls for human decency, equality and justice for all is the philosophy that will hold us together as humanity going into this 21st century.”

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair Campaign, the reparatory justice movement, said he believed Charles’s expressions of sorrow over slavery were sincere, but was disappointed he had not gone any further than his previous remarks.

“The apology hasn’t come. And there’s no talk about reparatory justice. So to that extent, this speech to me was a disappointment,” he said.

The king’s reference to support for health, education and infrastructure, Gonsalves said, concerned subjects already covered in the agreements in the UN sustainable development goals.

“What we are saying is that there has to be, additionally … a special carve-out in respect of reparatory justice,” he added.
output.standfirst: Speaking at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, Charles said his growing understanding of slavery's history had strengthened his resolve to address its legacy, though he stopped short of an apology or backing for reparations as demands grow.
output.progress: Burnham has proposed debt-reset talks for Commonwealth nations and announced £40m for Caribbean infrastructure, as officials discuss a reparatory justice dialogue.

output.headline: Courts uphold Guardian and ITN's right to publish sexual misconduct allegations
output.bodyHtml:
A “well-known individual” has failed in his attempt to stop two media organisations from publishing allegations of inappropriate sexual activities towards young women, the high court has ruled.

However, the judge in the case, Mr Justice Nicklin, found that it was for the state’s health services to protect the man, known in court only as PPT, from harm in the form of mental health treatment, rather than the court’s responsibility to protect him by stopping the Guardian and ITN from publishing the allegations, which he denies.

The legal team for the anonymous individual had claimed he was “highly likely” to attempt suicide if the allegations were published.

PPT’s legal team said he had attempted to kill himself twice since being contacted about the allegations in May. On the second occasion he absconded from a secure hospital to do so, they said.

Nicklin concluded he was satisfied that a decision to permit publication of the claims, the anticipation of publication and publication itself “would each materially increase the claimant’s risk of suicide”.

“That increase would be very substantial,” he said.

The claimant was seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

“The court has not assumed responsibility for the claimant’s psychiatric treatment or safety in the relevant sense,” Nicklin’s ruling states. “In the present case, the state has assumed responsibility for the claimant’s immediate safety through the psychiatric hospital and mental health services.

“The claimant is detained under the Mental Health Act 1983. The hospital exercises direct control over his care, observation, treatment, access to means of self-harm, leave and eventual discharge. It has assumed responsibility for the very risk with which article two is concerned.

“The evidence establishes that the hospital can provide significant protection. Inpatient treatment cannot eliminate the risk, but it materially reduces the likelihood of suicide.”

Nicklin said he had to balance the claimant’s rights with the media outlets’ right of freedom of expression.

The claimant had also made a claim under article eight of the ECHR about the impact his death, serious self-harm or a prolonged psychiatric admission would have upon his relationship with his son.

Nicklin said the claim had “very substantial weight”, but had to be balanced against the rights of the media companies to publish.

He said an injunction “would constitute an exceptionally serious interference” with their rights.

“It would prohibit the defendants from publishing the results of their investigations into allegations of serious wrongdoing by a prominent individual,” he found. “It would also prevent the sources whose accounts form part of those investigations from communicating their experiences to the public.”

The anonymity of the claimant remains in place because the judge granted him permission to appeal against the ruling.

Nicklin’s ruling stated that the Guardian and ITN allege that the claimant used his power and status as a well-known public figure to “establish contact with young women, who were also considerably younger than him, and engage, and/or seek to engage in inappropriate sexual activity”.

They claim the alleged incidents took place over several years and that some of them, if proved, could amount to criminal offences.

The judge emphasised that the current case did not examine whether the allegations against the claimant were true, but only whether the court should prevent the media outlets from publishing them.

He said the proposed journalism “did not lose its public interest value” merely because the allegations were disputed.

Nicklin also pointed to the implications of granting an injunction based on the risk of suicide.

“The principle contended for would apply whenever the court was satisfied that otherwise lawful publication would create a sufficiently grave risk of suicide or psychiatric harm and that restraint was the most effective means of preventing the trigger,” he found.

“The evidence does not identify a point at which publication would become safe merely through the passage of time. The relief sought would therefore be of uncertain and potentially indefinite duration.”

Nicklin rejected a proposal for the injunction to remain in place with a reassessment of the claimant’s condition after 18 months.

“The evidence does not … provide a clinical basis for selecting that or any other period for reassessment, or for concluding that treatment would by then have reduced the publication-related risk sufficiently,” he found.
output.standfirst: A high court judge rejected a 'well-known' man's attempt to block publication by citing suicide risk, ruling that his safety is the health service's responsibility, not the court's; his anonymity remains in place pending any appeal.
output.progress: NHS mental health services, not the courts, are responsible for protecting the claimant, who remains under psychiatric care in hospital.

output.headline: Trump to replace Israel's $4bn military aid with arms sales
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year, replacing it with arms sales instead, in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.

In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, the US president said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it”.

“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.

Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”

Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.

Israeli officials appeared to be taken by surprise by the announcement, and leading members of the opposition said it showed the damage that Netanyahu had done to the US-Israel relationship. The announcement comes at a crucial moment after Netanyahu’s party lost its majority in the Knesset in last week’s elections and the opposition is trying to cobble together a coalition to replace him.

“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right rival to Netanyahu who is seeking to replace him as prime minister. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”

“A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not dismantle it,” wrote Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats opposition party. “Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis, putting Israel’s future at risk.”

Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as foreign military financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.

Related: ‘Our aim is that children are protected’: besieged West Bank school fortifies its defences against settler violence

Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, in which US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.

Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”

During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.
output.standfirst: The president made a surprise election-day announcement, saying arms sales would replace the aid, which he argued Israel no longer needs — a shift Netanyahu's rivals say exposes the damage he has done to the US-Israel relationship.
output.progress: Netanyahu reportedly proposed the shift to arms sales himself, after previously suggesting a decade-long taper of US aid.

output.headline: MPs' committee calls for urgent funding decision to protect parliament
output.bodyHtml:
A cross-party Commons committee has urged MPs to act now on funding and governance of the Palace of Westminster's restoration, setting out a series of recommendations to get the stalled project moving.

Decisions about how and when to begin a full restoration of the building, which is Grade I-listed and a Unesco world heritage site, have been repeatedly delayed amid disagreement over how it should be done and rising costs.

The cost of maintaining the estate will soon hit £2m a week, and a recent estimate found the work could cost as much as £40bn and potentially last for six decades.

The cross-party Commons public accounts committee (PAC) said urgent action was needed to avoid the risk of a major fire or similar disaster, and to staunch increasing costs, with every year of inaction adding an estimated £420m to the restoration programme.

There has been a “political allergy” to making decisions, Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the Conservative MP who chairs the PAC, said.

As well as the ever-increasing costs, he said, MPs should also “imagine the blow suffered by the UK’s morale and reputation of some kind of catastrophic failure”.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he said.

“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks.”

The Victorian estate has been beset by problems that are kept in check only by ongoing maintenance, including regular plumbing failures, leaking roofs, crumbling masonry protected by a maze of scaffolding, and a persistent fire risk from outdated electrics — which is why round-the-clock fire patrols are already in place.

This has resulted in a maintenance bill of about £1.5m a week. The PAC report said that without action the figure was expected to reach £2m.

Related: Restoring Palace of Westminster could cost £40bn and take 61 years

The issue has been seen as a matter for MPs and peers to decide, rather than the government. The PAC stressed that it was not its role to recommend a particular programme, but the report urges action and sets out a series of recommendations for making the process work better.

It says that in the next six months the clerks of the Commons and the Lords – who are nominally in charge of the process – should set out a plan to properly engage parliamentarians, something it says has so far been lacking.

Other recommendations include a more robust set of cost estimates and a timetable to help a decision about the main project in 2030, as well as a more urgent approach to finalising temporary accommodation for both chambers while the works take place.

Calling the current governance of the scheme “far too complex”, it says the process should be made easier, and a new restoration and renewal select committee formed, allowing MPs to hold senior officials to account.

Four proposals for refurbishment, ranging from a nearly-full exit from the estate during the works to a version in which only the Lords would move, have been narrowed to two, from which MPs must choose.

The first, a “full decant”, would involve staff moving to buildings on the north side of the estate, with the Commons being put in Richmond House, a nearby government building, and the Lords to the QEII conference centre. The project would last up to 24 years and cost about £15.6bn.

A “staged decant” would last anything from 38 to 61 years and involve the Commons moving to the Lords chamber for up to two years. That project would cost about £39.2bn.

The report says there are particular worries about the temporary accommodation in terms of ensuring it is available and the cost.

It states that the estimate to refurbish the QEII centre of £417m, and a bill of about £2bn to set up the northern part of the estate for a decant, feel “very high”, noting that Canada had managed to install a temporary chamber as its parliamentary estate was refurbished for much less.

“We are concerned that the programme is being shaped around the availability of temporary accommodation, rather than temporary accommodation being delivered to meet the programme’s needs,” it said.

A parliament spokesperson said the report “provides welcome scrutiny”.

“The PAC concludes that without action, the Palace of Westminster will, at best, be in a process of managed decline,” they said. “Work is already happening across the parliamentary estate to ensure the ongoing safety of those working here and visiting.”
output.standfirst: A Commons report recommends clear cost estimates, a firm timetable and a new select committee to finally get the Palace of Westminster's restoration moving — as maintenance costs, now nearing £2m a week, keep climbing and delay keeps the building at risk.
output.progress: The public accounts committee wants a new select committee and a clear timetable to finally get the restoration programme moving.

output.headline: Cunha's late double caps stunning United comeback against Roma
output.bodyHtml:
Michael Carrick enjoyed one of his finest nights as a Manchester United player in the Champions League against Roma, scoring twice in a 7-1 win in the quarter-final, second leg in 2007. The re-run here was all about his managerial survival at the club – and United delivered a fightback to match it.

The situation had looked impossibly tough for him at half-time. Amid an atmosphere of continued fan anger towards the United ownership, Carrick’s team had been implausibly bad. Roma took a 2-0 lead into the break and the truth was that the scoreline greatly flattered United.

Related: ‘I wasn’t performing’: Bruno Fernandes says Carrick was right to drop him after criticism

What happened next was a fightback for the ages. For Carrick, it might even have topped 2007. United’s defending had been so loose, so generous. But they finally showed the other side to their game – the one about attacking punch; derring-do. They found a solution to their woes at the back. Keep the ball in the other half.

Matheus Cunha was the hero and it said plenty about the chaos of this tie, the wildness of the emotions, that he ended up being sent off for a second yellow card in the 90th minute. His lunge at Leonardo Balerdi was the definition of a rush of blood.

Before that, Cunha had supplemented a Bruno Fernandes penalty – which the captain converted after a retake – with a touch and finish in the 83rd minute following an error from Balerdi. Then came the coup de grace.

It was a burst from Kobbie Mainoo, who was positive on his return to the starting XI after injury, and a fizzed pass from the substitute, Shea Lacey. Cunha took the ball with a lovely first touch before flashing a shot in off the inside of the near post. Cunha likes to celebrate his goals with a surfing move. This time, having torn off his shirt, it was a surf in the crowd, which led to his first booking.

The United support sing about having seen it all. This was just extraordinary. Can it save Carrick? It was the team’s first win in 10 matches in all competitions so it was only a small step forward, even if it put United in a good position to qualify for the knockout rounds of the Champions League. In the heat of the moment, it felt like a giant one.

Carrick will go into Sunday’s Premier League game at home against Aston Villa – another must-win – with renewed belief. It was easy to say that his players had fought for him. As much as that, after all of the criticism of them, they fought for themselves.

Carrick had cut a relaxed figure at the pre-match press conference on Monday. He had seen some good signs, he insisted. There had been bursts. A win was coming. Nobody saw it at half-time, only yet more evidence of the defensive disasters that have blighted the season.

With Luke Shaw still injured, Carrick was forced to persist with Diogo Dalot out of position at left-back. Dalot pushed high at the outset, which felt bold. His positioning was pure folly on the opening Roma goal.

The visitors transitioned quickly and when Rodrigo Mora looked up from the inside left, all he could see was Matías Soulé in acres of space on the opposite channel. Where was Dalot? Mora played the pass. Soulé took a touch and swept past the exposed Senne Lammens.

United’s defending for the second goal was even worse. Leny Yoro turned and ran back towards his own goal as Roma advanced up the left and when the move appeared to have broken down for them around the United box, there was Harry Maguire to gift it back to Soulé with a dreadful miskick. He dropped his shoulder and shot; the ball hit Ayden Heaven’s hand and Donyell Malen converted from the penalty spot. Again, Dalot had been high up the pitch.

The mutiny could be felt before kick-off. The green and gold balloons of protest against the Glazers blew around the stadium. The sounds of it were everywhere; the chants against the club’s ownership a constant. When the clock showed 20 minutes and five seconds – or 2005; the year of the Glazer takeover – the Stretford End erupted in a planned move; hurling tennis balls down on to the pitch.

Moments earlier, a grisly Dalot error on the ball had almost led to Malen getting in for a third Roma goal and the first half was just an ordeal for United. Roma were well organised in their 3-4-2-1 shape and they got in up the right time and time again.

They might have had many more before the interval; Mora, Malen and Soulé all went close. United were so easy to play through. They were nervous on the ball. The lack of cohesion was glaring.

Related: Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames

Carrick was in the last chance saloon during half-time. Maybe United had nowhere further to fall. They rebelled. Carrick lost Carlos Baleba in the 46th minute after the midfielder pulled his hamstring as he shaped to shoot in a promising position. Then United caught a break – two, actually – and the mood shifted sharply.

It was a soft penalty award for a push by Gianluca Mancini on Cunha after he played a give-and-go with Fernandes. But when United had that sinking feeling after Fernandes saw his kick saved by Devis Vásquez, they were reprieved when the referee, Jesús Gil Manzano, ordered a retake for encroachment. Fernandes lashed home.

Bryan Mbeumo, played through by Cunha for a one-on-one with Vásquez, saw his shot hit one post and then the other one before refusing to cross the line.

United threatened from corners. Maguire went close. Dalot had a header cleared off the line. It was Dalot’s cross for Cunha’s equaliser – a reward for the full-back’s perseverance. Cunha’s winner was the prompt for bedlam.
output.progress: United fought back from 2-0 down at half-time, with Fernandes and Cunha scoring to complete the comeback.

output.headline: Hinton backs global push for mandatory AI safety testing
output.bodyHtml:
The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, one of the “godfathers of AI”, has told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks, and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future”.

But Hinton also said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology, as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next, such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.

Related: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’

Hinton, 78, said that within a decade and possibly sooner, humanity will know whether it can manage the technology’s risks and enable what he called “radical abundance” or whether “we fail to manage the risks and … have a huge gap between rich and poor, huge cultural problems, massive unemployment, just society being torn apart”.

Hinton was speaking before a screening of a new feature-length documentary, AI: Probably Nothing to Worry About – a title suggested by an AI chatbot – featuring him and his former Google colleague Demis Hassabis. Hinton tells the documentary makers: “I feel I have a duty. I’ve got a reputation that makes me a spokesperson and I need to burn it all on this.”

Speaking to the Guardian, Hinton took aim at the risk-taking by the leaders of some of the major AI companies who continue to release ever more powerful AI models as they race for supremacy and market-share, saying he didn’t trust Sam Altman, the chief executive of the ChatGPT maker, OpenAI, “at all”. “I think [Mark] Zuckerberg and [Elon] Musk and Sam Altman, they understand the risks, and they don’t give a shit. They’d rather have the money. That’s my belief.”

The London-born computer scientist, who grew up in Bristol and spent much of his career at the University of Toronto, said it was “extremely worrying” that Altman was in charge of one of the handful of frontier US AI companies currently leading a race with China to develop the most powerful AI. Altman insisted in September: “the world should trust we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing and because we feel the magnitude of this”.

Hinton has been working on AI for about 44 years and in the 1970s coined the concept of the neural network – a mathematical system that could learn and gain experience much like humans do. In 2023 he quit Google to speak freely about AI risks, saying: “If these things get carried away with getting more control, we’re in trouble.”

He said he viewed incidents this summer in which OpenAI AI agents conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website as akin to 1979’s partial nuclear meltdown at the Three Mile Island power station in Pennsylvania – effectively a warning shot.

“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chornobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he said.

This Chornobyl-type of event would not be a nuclear incident, according to the examples he gave, but rather could include an AI-enabled attack on the electricity-generating system that “causes a massive brownout” or an incident that brings down the financial system for a week.

“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.”

Asked who “they” were, he said: “world leaders other than Trump”.

Hinton backs a tougher plan endorsed by the president of Finland and 32 other countries, including Singapore, Germany, Canada and Australia, for mandatory testing of frontier AI models, independent evaluation and intergovernmental common standards. The US president, Donald Trump, has said he “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme” to control AI and wants frontier AI companies to regulate themselves, amid concern that rules could hinder the US in its AI race with China.

The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he will use the UK’s G20 presidency next year to seek agreement on a “single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks”.

Related: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer

Hinton said: “We need something like the American FDA for drugs where the companies have to give very good statistical evidence to an independent authority that [the AI model] does more good than harm before it is released. We discovered with thalidomide [a drug developed in the 1950s that caused severe birth defects] that releasing and then suing them isn’t the right way to do it. What the big tech companies are saying is treat it like we treated thalidomide.”

Hinton’s role as one of the progenitors of AI has led to comparisons to Robert Oppenheimer, who was central to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of Hinton’s friends even bought him an Oppenheimer-style hat. But he insists: “I was not Oppenheimer”, citing the thousands of other scientists also working in the same field of neural networks.

Despite his warnings, Hinton remains, on balance, hopeful that catastrophe can be averted.

“My gut is that we’re still in control,” he said. “We might well be able to do something. It’ll only work if we put a big effort into it, but we might well put a big effort into it.”
output.standfirst: The Nobel-winning 'godfather of AI' backs a global testing plan endorsed by Finland and dozens of other countries, cautions that a major AI-related incident is likely within a year or two, and says humanity might have been better off never developing the technology, while accusing industry leaders of ignoring the risks for profit.
